ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200) Spectroscopy Thermogravimetry Photophysics

ABSTRACT Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have gained significant interest among researchers in the past two decades due to their improved physical and chemical characteristics beyond traditional organic solvents. They represent a recent advancement in eco-friendly solvents. Studying their physical characteristics would thus be very beneficial for designing methods in varied application domains. A majority of DESs are traditionally categorized into several types. Amongst them, the recently known Type V DESs have received increased attention. They are made using nonionic precursors that frequently exhibit marginal high vapor pressure and lower viscosities than their ionic equivalents and are chloride-free. In this study, four new PEGylated DESs are successfully prepared by using polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200) as a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) with varied organic acids such as levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) in different molar ratios. Various atomic interactions between the HBAs and HBD in these prepared DESs were explained using Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and ¹H- and ¹³C-nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H- and ¹³C NMR) spectroscopy. Also, the temperature-induced transition in the prepared DESs was recorded using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The thermophysical properties, such as density (ρ) and viscosity (η), were defined as a function of temperature. Also, the study investigates the physical and chemical properties of PEGylated DESs, focusing on their dipolarity/polarizability, solvatochromic behavior, chemical structure, and composition. It uses Kamlet-Taft parameters to explore the H-bond donor and acceptor tendency and understand the role of acidic constituents. The study also investigates the solvation dynamics and diffusion of fluorescence quenching of pyrene and benzo [a]pyrene using nitromethane as a quencher. Here, the fluorescence lifetime adheres to the Stern–Volmer fitting, and higher bimolecular quenching rate constants support the faster diffusion of fluorophore and quencher molecules in these PEGylated DESs compared to other hydrophilic DESs. The study establishes constituent dependence and faster solvation dynamics.

# 1. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are composed of hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) having low lattice energy, held together due to the formation of H-bonding, resulting in a significant decrease in the melting point of the mixture compared to the individual components [1,2]. Along with the intricate H-bonding interaction, the ionic interactions, van der Waals forces, and the entropy

of mixing also play a substantial role in the formation and depression in the melting point of DESS [2]. Over time, different kinds of DESs have been prepared using various compounds. Based on this, DESs are cate- gorized into four primary groups according to their components: Type I includes quarternary ammonium salts and metal chloride. However, their utilization is limited by the high moisture sensitivity of these sol- vents. Type II consists of a quaternary ammonium salt and metal chloride hydrate. This class of DESs has acquired immense popularity because it is readily available in large libraries of constituents and their low toxicity. Type IV DESs comprise a metal chloride hydrate and an organic molecule. Type V DESs include nonionic molecules as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD). In contrast to Type III DESs, Type V DESs are mostly non-polar due to the hydrophobic nature of the constituents consisting of long alkyl chains. Although the ionic contribution is absent, they exhibit a significant depression in their melting point due to prevalent H-bonding [3]. These DESs are often acknowledged as a class of ionic liquids (ILs) as they possess similar characteristics, which include high thermal stability, low volatility, low vapor pressures, and tunable polarity. Unlike ILs, inclined to be expen- sive, non-biodegradable, and highly toxic, DESs are typically safe, inexpensive, sustainable, biodegradable, non-toxic, and easy to prepare [3]. Such a wide range of observed properties enables DESs to replace the existing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are potentially used widely throughout the research and industrial sectors.

Given the immense number of combinations of HBA and HBDs, obtaining the optimal DES requires an exhaustive trial-and-error through many possible binary combinations. Such an outlook ob- structs the adaptation of DESs for specific applications and effectively avoids many potential advantages that DESs offer. Though in the last two decades, DESs have gained significant research interest in biotech- nology applications [4], flexible thermal sensors [5], CO2 capture and conversion [6], surfactant self-assembly [7], formation of hydrophobic eutectogels [8], antimicrobial activity [9], liquid-liquid microextraction method [10], electrochemical process [11]. Despite numerous studies, there is still insufficient information covering the formation and char- acteristics of DESs.

DESs composed of nonionic compounds are simply considered to be ideal mixtures [12]. For instance, in the polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200)-carboxylic acid system, a strong interaction arises due to the difference in acidity between the ether group and aliphatic hydroxyl and carboxylic groups of acids [13,14]. These DESs are considered inex- pensive and offer eco-friendly preferences due to the presence of PEG components. They have been widely used as efficient absorbents for separating nitrogen and sulfur impurities from fuels [15] and recovering metals [16]. Additionally, PEGylated DESs are very effective solvents in material synthesis [17,18]. Amarpreet Singh et al. produced DESs by incorporating glycerol and PEG with choline chloride (ChCl) at different molar ratios. Their investigation has shown that the thermophysical characteristics of DESs may be tailored by altering the type of HBDs and controlling the molar ratios [13]. Filipa Lima et al. formulated various DESs utilizing PEG and its precursors and evaluated their efficacy in extracting sulfur compounds from a model fuel [15].

Before DESs and conventional solvents are compared to be employed industrially, it is necessary to quantify their solvation characteristics, such as H-bonding ability and polarity, along with the discernible physical parameters, for instance, melting point, boiling temperature, and density. The most comprehensive and widely exercised quantitative assessment of solvent photophysical characteristics is the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameter set that measures the acidity (hydrogen bond donating ability), basicity (hydrogen bond accepting ability), and dipolarity/ polarizability. In this regard, quenching of fluorescence is one of the most reliable tools for getting insight into any newly developed solvent system. It offers a practical method to gain an understanding of accessibility dynamics and solute solvation behaviour within a solubilizing medium. In this direction, frequently used neutral fluorescence probes are pyrene and its derivatives [19,20].

In the current study, we attempt to prepare four DES systems based on PEG200 as an HBD and organic carboxylic acids, i.e., levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as HBAs. Various thermophysical characteristics, such as viscosity, density, and other associated properties, were measured for PEGylated DESs. Spectroscopic techniques like FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR were

employed to develop a comprehensive and clear understanding of the variations in solute-solvent interactions within the examined PEGylated DESs. To investigate the stability and thermal behavior of PEGylated DESs, thermogravimetric (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analyses were performed. UV-Vis absorbance and fluorescent probes estimated the corresponding empirical parameters based on their solvatochromic responses. Also, we have investigated the fluorescence quenching of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with nitro-methane as a fluorescence quencher as a function of temperature. UV-Vis probes such as 4-nitroaniline (NA), N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (DENA), and Nile Red (NR) were employed to calculate Kamlet-Taft parameters.

## 2. Experimental ### 2.1. Materials Polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200, 99.0%) was acquired from SDFCL Pvt. Ltd., INDIA. Levulinic acid (LA, 98.0%), cinnamic acid (CIA, 99.0%), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA, 99.0%), and citric acid (CA, 99.0%) were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich, INDIA. Pyrene (99.0%) and benzo[a]pyrene (99.0%) were procured from Sigma-Aldrich, INDIA, and Accustandard, USA, respectively, and preserved in moisture-free conditions. Ethanol (99.9%) and dichloromethane (99.0%), used for stock solutions preparation of probes, were obtained from Merck, INDIA, and Sigma-Aldrich Co., INDIA, respectively. Nitromethane (99.0%) was purchased from Acros Organics, INDIA. 4-nitroaniline (NA, 99.0%) and N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (DENA, 99.0 %) were purchased from Spectrochem Co. Ltd., INDIA and Frinton Laboratories, USA respectively, and Nile Red (NR, >=98% (HPLC)) was procured from Sigma-Aldrich, INDIA. The pure components were combined at a specific molar ratio (mentioned in Table 1), and the mixture was stirred at 333.15 K and 150 rpm until a clear and homogenous liquid was obtained. For weighing, Mettler-Toledo AB104-S balance (accuracy ±0.0001 g) was used. To prevent any alterations in the structure and physical characteristics of the DESs, the sample preparation underwent an environment controlled for moisture levels and stored in sealed containers. ## 2.5. Solution flow study The density (ρ) and viscosity (η) of the prepared DESs were determined simultaneously using a digital density meter by Anton Paar (model: SVM 3001 viscometer). To ensure accuracy, this instrument was cleaned with ethanol and then toluene before and after each measurement session. The meter boasts a ρ repeatability of ±0.00005 g m⁻³. Given the high sensitivity of ρ to temperature changes, the integrated Peltier device proved crucial for temperature control during the measurements. Here, the temperature was maintained with an accuracy of ±0.1 K.

2.6. *Photophysics study* The stock solution of probes was prepared by the dissolution of the required quantity of each probe in ethanol and dichloromethane, and they were stored in clean amber glass vials at 277.15 K (4 °C). The required volume of stock solution was taken in a quartz cuvette with a 1 cm path length, and the solvent was evaporated using highly pure grade 1 nitrogen. The pre-requisite DES amount was transferred to the cuvette.

UV-Vis absorbance spectra of DENA, NA, and NR were collected using a Lambda 35 double beam spectrometer (procured from PerkinElmer) that has a modifiable bandwidth and contains deuterium and xenon lamps and a photomultiplier tube (PMT) detector.

The steady-state fluorescence spectra were acquired on the instru- ment (purchased from Edinburg Instruments Ltd.) with an FLS1000 spectrometer that is outfitted with STGM325-M emission mono- chromators and STGM325-X grating excitation and contains a 450 W xenon arc lamp as a source of radiation, a red PMT detector and a quantum northwest luma 40 to control temperature. Before data anal- ysis in Sigma Plot v14 software, all the spectra were properly corrected by subtracting the optical responses from appropriate blanks. Inner filter correction in fluorescence intensities was done according to Eq. (S11).

Time-resolved excited-state intensity decay measurements of pyrene were acquired using Horiba-Jobin Yvon, Inc., fluoro cube time-correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) fluorimeter. 340 nm UV-pulsed nano LED-340 source having a pulse width <1.0 ns was used to excite the probe. DAQ-MCA-3 series (P7882) multichannel analyser was exercised to collect data. The software subtracted the instrument response function (IRF) of a scattering solution of glycogen in water. The excited-state intensity decays were analyzed using DAS6 analysis software and were fitted to desired decay models.

3.2. Thermal analysis Studies have reported the thermal stability evaluation of DESs to be one of the most crucial subjects of research. For instance, Ayoub et al. utilized TGA/ DTG techniques and deduced that the thermal stability of DESs is more significantly impacted by HBD than HBA. They observed that a longer alkyl chain in HBD enhances the thermal stability of DES. Moreover, they determined that as the proportion of HBD in DES increases, its thermal stability tends to decrease [27]. The significance of viscosity (η) lies in its impact on the transport phenomena of fluids [36]. Also, η profoundly affects the movement of dissolved particles within the solvent. Therefore, a better understanding of η is a crucial approach in determining the suitability of fluid for various applications. However, their high η is a significant disadvantage. The primary reason for the high η of DESs is their extensive H-bond network that restricts the mobility of free species within the solvent. This information is widely accepted in the scientific community [32,37].

The experimental η data for all PEGylated DESs solutions were observed at various temperatures and are illustrated in Fig. 5 and Table S1. Based on our experimental results, it can be inferred that the CA: PEG has a much greater viscosity value when compared to the remaining three DESs. When the temperature rises, the η tends to decrease significantly. An Arrhenius model was utilized to fit the η data. Eq. (S9) shows the relationship between η and T for the four different DESs. Fig. S2 shows the curves of log η plotted against 1/T for each of the four prepared DESs [32].

The measurements of η for PEGylated DES solutions were conducted over a range of temperature from 283.15 to 363.15 K. To study the temperature-dependent η behavior of these DES, the Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann (VFT) model was used. The VFT model is represented by Eq. (S10). According to the results, an increase in temperature resulted in a decrease in η. This can be explained by decreased H-bonding interactions between the DESs complexes as the temperature increases. It is well-established that the longer excited-state lifetime allows the mutual approach of M* (excited pyrene molecule) and Q (quencher molecule). The bimolecular excited-state event is thus controlled by diffusion, and this type of quenching is called dynamic quenching [19].

At each of the investigated temperatures for every DES investigated (Fig. 9), the linear plots of τ₀/τ versus [Q] (quencher concentration) demonstrate the dynamic nature of fluorescence quenching resulting in equivalent Stern–Volmer quenching constant (Ksv) and dynamic quenching constant (KD) calucated using equations S16 and S17. The comparatively lower dynamic η of LA: PEG and HCA: PEG supports faster diffusion and dynamics of pyrene-nitromethane fluorophore- quencher pair, thereby increasing the rate of bimolecular quenching process in these DESs as compared to CA: PEG and other DESs of com- parable η. Thus, the estimated kq values follow the opposite trend as the η of DESs. These observations simply establish the role of dynamic η in facilitating the diffusion of the excited pyrene molecule and the nitromethane.

It can be seen that Ea for CA: PEG is significantly higher in comparison to other documented systems [49]. This observation further supports the slow diffusion of nitromethane and excited pyrene in CA: PEG DES. The lower Ea values in LA: PEG and HCA: PEG imply more facile quenching dynamics in these DESs. ## 4. Conclusion The PEGylated DESs were effectively prepared using varied molar ratios. Studies on their thermophysical properties revealed that by modifying the type of HBDs and adjusting the molar ratios, the properties of the DESs can be tailored. The interaction between the HBAs and HBD is inferred from the FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR spectroscopy. The TGA technique is utilized to evaluate the thermal stability of prepared DESs. At the same time, DSC revealed the formation of the stable DES across a broad temperature range. For these DESs, the ρ and η decrease with increases the temperature. Also, the calculated thermophysical and its associated properties from the data of ρ and η. Here, the LA: PEG system exhibits high values of S° and Uᴘᴏᴛ, indicating that it is a highly stable DES compared to other DESs. We have employed Kamlet-Taft parameters and dynamic quenching of fluorescent probes to unveil some of the solvation characteristics of the DESs under investigation. Empirical dipolarity values (π*), supported by I₁/I₃ data of pyrene dissolved in all three DESs, were found to be highest for CA: PEG and followed by LA: PEG and HCA: PEG, respectively. The capacity of DESs investigated to donate H-bond to the solute is higher than some DESs and alcohols but slightly lower than water. Within PEGylated DESs investigated in this work, pyrene fluorescence and its quenching by nitromethane are helpful in revealing structural information and solute diffusion kinetics. Since these DESs do not support the excimer formation of pyrene, solvent–solute interactions can be studied through diffusion-controlled

quenching of pyrene. Excited-state intensity decay of pyrene in the presence and the absence of a quencher shows a double exponential decay quencher regardless of temperature (298.15 K-338.15 K) and chemical constituents of DESs. The linear plots of το/τ versus [Q] indi- cate that the fluorescence quenching is purely dynamic. As a result, the recovered Stern-Volmer dynamic quenching rate constant (Ksy) and bimolecular quenching rate constant (kq) for the pyrene-nitromethane fluorophore-quencher pair in the temperature range of 298.15-338.15 K is lowest for CA: PEG owing to its highest η in this temperature range. Also, the higher η of CA: PEG demands higher acti- vation energy Ea (50.0 ± 1.7 kJ mol⁻¹), even higher than Reline (42.4 ± 1.8 kJ mol⁻¹). In addition to providing insights into the structural characteristics and diffusion dynamics inside the hydrophobic DES, multidimensional pyrene fluorescence also establishes the DES as a solubilizing milieu, a cost-effective, ecologically friendly nonpolar media that can be used globally.

They represent a recent advancement in eco-friendly solvents. Studying their physical characteristics would thus be very beneficial for designing methods in varied application domains. A majority of DESs are traditionally categorized into several types. Amongst them, the recently known Type V DESs have received increased attention. They are made using nonionic precursors that frequently exhibit marginal high vapor pressure and lower viscosities than their ionic equivalents and are chloride-free. In this study, four new PEGylated DESs are successfully prepared by using polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200) as a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) with varied organic acids such as levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) in different molar ratios. Various atomic interactions between the HBAs and HBD in these prepared DESs were explained using Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and ¹H- and ¹³C-nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H- and ¹³C NMR) spectroscopy. Also, the temperature-induced transition in the prepared DESs was recorded using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The thermophysical properties, such as density (ρ) and viscosity (η), were defined as a function of temperature. Also, the study investigates the physical and chemical properties of PEGylated DESs, focusing on their dipolarity/polarizability, solvatochromic behavior, chemical structure, and composition. It uses Kamlet-Taft parameters to explore the H-bond donor and acceptor tendency and understand the role of acidic constituents. The study also investigates the solvation dynamics and diffusion of fluorescence quenching of pyrene and benzo [a]pyrene using nitromethane as a quencher. Here, the fluorescence lifetime adheres to the Stern–Volmer fitting, and higher bimolecular quenching rate constants support the faster diffusion of fluorophore and quencher molecules in these PEGylated DESs compared to other hydrophilic DESs. The study establishes constituent dependence and faster solvation dynamics. # 1. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are composed of hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) having low lattice energy, held together due to the formation of H-bonding, resulting in a significant decrease in the melting point of the mixture compared to the individual components [1,2]. Along with the intricate H-bonding interaction, the ionic interactions, van der Waals forces, and the entropy of mixing also play a substantial role in the formation and depression in the melting point of DESS [2]. Over time, different kinds of DESs have been prepared using various compounds. Based on this, DESs are cate- gorized into four primary groups according to their components: Type I includes quarternary ammonium salts and metal chloride. However, their utilization is limited by the high moisture sensitivity of these sol- vents. Type II consists of a quaternary ammonium salt and metal chloride hydrate. This class of DESs has acquired immense popularity because it is readily available in large libraries of constituents and their low toxicity. Type IV DESs comprise a metal chloride hydrate and an organic molecule. Type V DESs include nonionic molecules as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD). In contrast to Type III DESs, Type V DESs are mostly non-polar due to the hydrophobic nature of the constituents consisting of long alkyl chains. Although the ionic contribution is absent, they exhibit a significant depression in their melting point due to prevalent H-bonding [3]. These DESs are often acknowledged as a class of ionic liquids (ILs) as they possess similar characteristics, which include high thermal stability, low volatility, low vapor pressures, and tunable polarity. Unlike ILs, inclined to be expen- sive, non-biodegradable, and highly toxic, DESs are typically safe, inexpensive, sustainable, biodegradable, non-toxic, and easy to prepare [3]. Such a wide range of observed properties enables DESs to replace the existing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are potentially used widely throughout the research and industrial sectors. Given the immense number of combinations of HBA and HBDs, obtaining the optimal DES requires an exhaustive trial-and-error through many possible binary combinations. Such an outlook ob- structs the adaptation of DESs for specific applications and effectively avoids many potential advantages that DESs offer. Though in the last two decades, DESs have gained significant research interest in biotech- nology applications [4], flexible thermal sensors [5], CO2 capture and conversion [6], surfactant self-assembly [7], formation of hydrophobic eutectogels [8], antimicrobial activity [9], liquid-liquid microextraction method [10], electrochemical process [11]. Despite numerous studies, there is still insufficient information covering the formation and char- acteristics of DESs. DESs composed of nonionic compounds are simply considered to be ideal mixtures [12]. For instance, in the polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200)-carboxylic acid system, a strong interaction arises due to the difference in acidity between the ether group and aliphatic hydroxyl and carboxylic groups of acids [13,14]. These DESs are considered inex- pensive and offer eco-friendly preferences due to the presence of PEG components. They have been widely used as efficient absorbents for separating nitrogen and sulfur impurities from fuels [15] and recovering metals [16]. Additionally, PEGylated DESs are very effective solvents in material synthesis [17,18]. Amarpreet Singh et al. produced DESs by incorporating glycerol and PEG with choline chloride (ChCl) at different molar ratios. Their investigation has shown that the thermophysical characteristics of DESs may be tailored by altering the type of HBDs and controlling the molar ratios [13]. Filipa Lima et al. formulated various DESs utilizing PEG and its precursors and evaluated their efficacy in extracting sulfur compounds from a model fuel [15]. Before DESs and conventional solvents are compared to be employed industrially, it is necessary to quantify their solvation characteristics, such as H-bonding ability and polarity, along with the discernible physical parameters, for instance, melting point, boiling temperature, and density. The most comprehensive and widely exercised quantitative assessment of solvent photophysical characteristics is the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameter set that measures the acidity (hydrogen bond donating ability), basicity (hydrogen bond accepting ability), and dipolarity/ polarizability. In this regard, quenching of fluorescence is one of the most reliable tools for getting insight into any newly developed solvent system. It offers a practical method to gain an understanding of accessibility dynamics and solute solvation behaviour within a solubilizing medium. In this direction, frequently used neutral fluorescence probes are pyrene and its derivatives [19,20]. In the current study, we attempt to prepare four DES systems based on PEG200 as an HBD and organic carboxylic acids, i.e., levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as HBAs. Various thermophysical characteristics, such as viscosity, density, and other associated properties, were measured for PEGylated DESs. Spectroscopic techniques like FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR were employed to develop a comprehensive and clear understanding of the variations in solute-solvent interactions within the examined PEGylated DESs. To investigate the stability and thermal behavior of PEGylated DESs, thermogravimetric (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analyses were performed. UV-Vis absorbance and fluorescent probes estimated the corresponding empirical parameters based on their solvatochromic responses. Also, we have investigated the fluorescence quenching of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with nitro-methane as a fluorescence quencher as a function of temperature. UV-Vis probes such as 4-nitroaniline (NA), N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (DENA), and Nile Red (NR) were employed to calculate Kamlet-Taft parameters. ## 2. Experimental ### 2.1. ## 4. Conclusion The PEGylated DESs were effectively prepared using varied molar ratios. Studies on their thermophysical properties revealed that by modifying the type of HBDs and adjusting the molar ratios, the properties of the DESs can be tailored. The interaction between the HBAs and HBD is inferred from the FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR spectroscopy. The TGA technique is utilized to evaluate the thermal stability of prepared DESs. At the same time, DSC revealed the formation of the stable DES across a broad temperature range. For these DESs, the ρ and η decrease with increases the temperature. Also, the calculated thermophysical and its associated properties from the data of ρ and η. Here, the LA: PEG system exhibits high values of S° and Uᴘᴏᴛ, indicating that it is a highly stable DES compared to other DESs. We have employed Kamlet-Taft parameters and dynamic quenching of fluorescent probes to unveil some of the solvation characteristics of the DESs under investigation. Empirical dipolarity values (π*), supported by I₁/I₃ data of pyrene dissolved in all three DESs, were found to be highest for CA: PEG and followed by LA: PEG and HCA: PEG, respectively. The capacity of DESs investigated to donate H-bond to the solute is higher than some DESs and alcohols but slightly lower than water. Within PEGylated DESs investigated in this work, pyrene fluorescence and its quenching by nitromethane are helpful in revealing structural information and solute diffusion kinetics. Since these DESs do not support the excimer formation of pyrene, solvent–solute interactions can be studied through diffusion-controlled quenching of pyrene. Excited-state intensity decay of pyrene in the presence and the absence of a quencher shows a double exponential decay quencher regardless of temperature (298.15 K-338.15 K) and chemical constituents of DESs. The linear plots of το/τ versus [Q] indi- cate that the fluorescence quenching is purely dynamic. As a result, the recovered Stern-Volmer dynamic quenching rate constant (Ksy) and bimolecular quenching rate constant (kq) for the pyrene-nitromethane fluorophore-quencher pair in the temperature range of 298.15-338.15 K is lowest for CA: PEG owing to its highest η in this temperature range. Also, the higher η of CA: PEG demands higher acti- vation energy Ea (50.0 ± 1.7 kJ mol⁻¹), even higher than Reline (42.4 ± 1.8 kJ mol⁻¹). In addition to providing insights into the structural characteristics and diffusion dynamics inside the hydrophobic DES, multidimensional pyrene fluorescence also establishes the DES as a solubilizing milieu, a cost-effective, ecologically friendly nonpolar media that can be used globally. They represent a recent advancement in eco-friendly solvents. Studying their physical characteristics would thus be very beneficial for designing methods in varied application domains. A majority of DESs are traditionally categorized into several types. Amongst them, the recently known Type V DESs have received increased attention. They are made using nonionic precursors that frequently exhibit marginal high vapor pressure and lower viscosities than their ionic equivalents and are chloride-free. In this study, four new PEGylated DESs are successfully prepared by using polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200) as a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) with varied organic acids such as levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) in different molar ratios. Various atomic interactions between the HBAs and HBD in these prepared DESs were explained using Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and ¹H- and ¹³C-nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H- and ¹³C NMR) spectroscopy. Also, the temperature-induced transition in the prepared DESs was recorded using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The thermophysical properties, such as density (ρ) and viscosity (η), were defined as a function of temperature. Also, the study investigates the physical and chemical properties of PEGylated DESs, focusing on their dipolarity/polarizability, solvatochromic behavior, chemical structure, and composition. It uses Kamlet-Taft parameters to explore the H-bond donor and acceptor tendency and understand the role of acidic constituents. The study also investigates the solvation dynamics and diffusion of fluorescence quenching of pyrene and benzo [a]pyrene using nitromethane as a quencher. Here, the fluorescence lifetime adheres to the Stern–Volmer fitting, and higher bimolecular quenching rate constants support the faster diffusion of fluorophore and quencher molecules in these PEGylated DESs compared to other hydrophilic DESs. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are composed of hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD) having low lattice energy, held together due to the formation of H-bonding, resulting in a significant decrease in the melting point of the mixture compared to the individual components [1,2]. Along with the intricate H-bonding interaction, the ionic interactions, van der Waals forces, and the entropy of mixing also play a substantial role in the formation and depression in the melting point of DESS [2]. Over time, different kinds of DESs have been prepared using various compounds. Based on this, DESs are cate- gorized into four primary groups according to their components: Type I includes quarternary ammonium salts and metal chloride. However, their utilization is limited by the high moisture sensitivity of these sol- vents. Type II consists of a quaternary ammonium salt and metal chloride hydrate. This class of DESs has acquired immense popularity because it is readily available in large libraries of constituents and their low toxicity. Type IV DESs comprise a metal chloride hydrate and an organic molecule. Type V DESs include nonionic molecules as hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen bond donor (HBD). In contrast to Type III DESs, Type V DESs are mostly non-polar due to the hydrophobic nature of the constituents consisting of long alkyl chains. Although the ionic contribution is absent, they exhibit a significant depression in their melting point due to prevalent H-bonding [3]. These DESs are often acknowledged as a class of ionic liquids (ILs) as they possess similar characteristics, which include high thermal stability, low volatility, low vapor pressures, and tunable polarity. Unlike ILs, inclined to be expen- sive, non-biodegradable, and highly toxic, DESs are typically safe, inexpensive, sustainable, biodegradable, non-toxic, and easy to prepare [3]. Such a wide range of observed properties enables DESs to replace the existing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are potentially used widely throughout the research and industrial sectors. Given the immense number of combinations of HBA and HBDs, obtaining the optimal DES requires an exhaustive trial-and-error through many possible binary combinations. Such an outlook ob- structs the adaptation of DESs for specific applications and effectively avoids many potential advantages that DESs offer. Though in the last two decades, DESs have gained significant research interest in biotech- nology applications [4], flexible thermal sensors [5], CO2 capture and conversion [6], surfactant self-assembly [7], formation of hydrophobic eutectogels [8], antimicrobial activity [9], liquid-liquid microextraction method [10], electrochemical process [11]. Despite numerous studies, there is still insufficient information covering the formation and char- acteristics of DESs. DESs composed of nonionic compounds are simply considered to be ideal mixtures [12]. For instance, in the polyethylene glycol 200 (PEG200)-carboxylic acid system, a strong interaction arises due to the difference in acidity between the ether group and aliphatic hydroxyl and carboxylic groups of acids [13,14]. These DESs are considered inex- pensive and offer eco-friendly preferences due to the presence of PEG components. They have been widely used as efficient absorbents for separating nitrogen and sulfur impurities from fuels [15] and recovering metals [16]. Additionally, PEGylated DESs are very effective solvents in material synthesis [17,18]. Amarpreet Singh et al. produced DESs by incorporating glycerol and PEG with choline chloride (ChCl) at different molar ratios. Their investigation has shown that the thermophysical characteristics of DESs may be tailored by altering the type of HBDs and controlling the molar ratios [13]. Filipa Lima et al. formulated various DESs utilizing PEG and its precursors and evaluated their efficacy in extracting sulfur compounds from a model fuel [15]. Before DESs and conventional solvents are compared to be employed industrially, it is necessary to quantify their solvation characteristics, such as H-bonding ability and polarity, along with the discernible physical parameters, for instance, melting point, boiling temperature, and density. The most comprehensive and widely exercised quantitative assessment of solvent photophysical characteristics is the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameter set that measures the acidity (hydrogen bond donating ability), basicity (hydrogen bond accepting ability), and dipolarity/ polarizability. In this regard, quenching of fluorescence is one of the most reliable tools for getting insight into any newly developed solvent system. It offers a practical method to gain an understanding of accessibility dynamics and solute solvation behaviour within a solubilizing medium. In this direction, frequently used neutral fluorescence probes are pyrene and its derivatives [19,20]. In the current study, we attempt to prepare four DES systems based on PEG200 as an HBD and organic carboxylic acids, i.e., levulinic acid (LA), cinnamic acid (CIA), hydrocinnamic acid (HCA), and citric acid (CA) as HBAs. Various thermophysical characteristics, such as viscosity, density, and other associated properties, were measured for PEGylated DESs. Spectroscopic techniques like FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR were employed to develop a comprehensive and clear understanding of the variations in solute-solvent interactions within the examined PEGylated DESs. To investigate the stability and thermal behavior of PEGylated DESs, thermogravimetric (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analyses were performed. UV-Vis absorbance and fluorescent probes estimated the corresponding empirical parameters based on their solvatochromic responses. Also, we have investigated the fluorescence quenching of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) with nitro-methane as a fluorescence quencher as a function of temperature. ## 4. Conclusion The PEGylated DESs were effectively prepared using varied molar ratios. Studies on their thermophysical properties revealed that by modifying the type of HBDs and adjusting the molar ratios, the properties of the DESs can be tailored. The interaction between the HBAs and HBD is inferred from the FT-IR, ¹H- and ¹³C NMR spectroscopy. The TGA technique is utilized to evaluate the thermal stability of prepared DESs. At the same time, DSC revealed the formation of the stable DES across a broad temperature range. For these DESs, the ρ and η decrease with increases the temperature. Also, the calculated thermophysical and its associated properties from the data of ρ and η. Here, the LA: PEG system exhibits high values of S° and Uᴘᴏᴛ, indicating that it is a highly stable DES compared to other DESs. We have employed Kamlet-Taft parameters and dynamic quenching of fluorescent probes to unveil some of the solvation characteristics of the DESs under investigation. Empirical dipolarity values (π*), supported by I₁/I₃ data of pyrene dissolved in all three DESs, were found to be highest for CA: PEG and followed by LA: PEG and HCA: PEG, respectively. The capacity of DESs investigated to donate H-bond to the solute is higher than some DESs and alcohols but slightly lower than water. Within PEGylated DESs investigated in this work, pyrene fluorescence and its quenching by nitromethane are helpful in revealing structural information and solute diffusion kinetics. Since these DESs do not support the excimer formation of pyrene, solvent–solute interactions can be studied through diffusion-controlled quenching of pyrene. Excited-state intensity decay of pyrene in the presence and the absence of a quencher shows a double exponential decay quencher regardless of temperature (298.15 K-338.15 K) and chemical constituents of DESs. The linear plots of το/τ versus [Q] indi- cate that the fluorescence quenching is purely dynamic. As a result, the recovered Stern-Volmer dynamic quenching rate constant (Ksy) and bimolecular quenching rate constant (kq) for the pyrene-nitromethane fluorophore-quencher pair in the temperature range of 298.15-338.15 K is lowest for CA: PEG owing to its highest η in this temperature range. Also, the higher η of CA: PEG demands higher acti- vation energy Ea (50.0 ± 1.7 kJ mol⁻¹), even higher than Reline (42.4 ± 1.8 kJ mol⁻¹). In addition to providing insights into the structural characteristics and diffusion dynamics inside the hydrophobic DES, multidimensional pyrene fluorescence also establishes the DES as a solubilizing milieu, a cost-effective, ecologically friendly nonpolar media that can be used globally.
